“Trump was in bed with Jensen”: Critics balk at Huang’s wish to return to Nvidia

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
  • Industry observers note that “Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged.
  • Recent findings suggest that right now, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “horrible idea.” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

Industry observers note that “Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Substantial Tech.”.

Recent findings suggest that right now, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “horrible idea.” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the organization it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.

Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported.

Sources indicate that if Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.

Sources indicate that “Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”.

What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who blueprint to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.”.

Industry observers note that “I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”.

According to recent reports, yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.

According to recent reports, the White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported. He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.

Industry observers note that other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom.

It has been revealed that “It is not just an intelligence concern; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal mentioned. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.”.

Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio.

It has been revealed that other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.”.

“The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth noted. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said.

“White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said.

If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth stated.

Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang promptly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported.

Sources indicate that also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. Citing Sacks’ alignment with Huang, TOP reported that after just one meeting with the two men, Trump decided to allow Nvidia to sell AI chips to China that the Biden administration had previously blocked.

According to recent reports, huang valued his alliance with Sacks, TOP noted, citing reporting that showed Huang declaring last year that Nvidia was “lucky” to have Sacks advising Trump. But TOP is concerned that the alliance was built on mutual financial interest and that Sacks took a part-time role in the Trump administration to avoid divestments or disclosure requirements that might have revealed the extent of his possible conflicts of interest.

TOP flagged two areas it believes warrant Congressional investigation. While advising Trump to embrace AI deregulation, Sacks and his firm, Craft Ventures, continued investing substantially in AI. Sacks also stood to benefit from pushing Trump to integrate AI into warfare and national security tools, TOP’s report said. Craft Ventures has invested in Palantir, “a Peter Thiel-founded government contractor seen as a ‘rising star’ in the US Defense Tech World and holding hundreds of millions in US government defense contracts,” TOP said.

Even within the Trump administration, officials have turned on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, seemingly looking to blame him for mishandling the Nvidia spying investigation and allowing Trump to maintain close ties with Huang despite apparent intelligence risks.

Lutnick has bragged publicly that he promised Huang “really easy access to the President” after joining the administration, TOP reported. That alliance helped push Trump to approve the sale of Nvidia H200s to China, TOP noted. And that seemed to directly benefit Lutnick, TOP said, because before he was confirmed as secretary, he was CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, which held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock.

“In his role as Secretary, Lutnick is responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals, like China,” TOP reported. “Lutnick and the company he controls benefited greatly from opening sales of Nvidia chips to China.”.

After Lutnick was required to hand that company over to his son, Cantor Fitzgerald “maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives,” TOP noted.

Industry observers note that those investments shifted substantially around the same time that Lutnick began facing pressure to “crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm suspected of funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China,” TOP reported. Cantor Fitzgerald “reduced its Nvidia holdings by nearly 50 percent between September 2025 and March 2026,” TOP noted.

Industry observers note that however, when Trump was reportedly first told of the spying allegations this spring, Cantor Fitzgerald again continued to boost Nvidia. Most prominently, the tech giant helped “finance the expansion of one of Nvidia’s newest business partners, IREN,” facilitating a five-year, $3.4 billion deal between Nvidia and the Australia-based cloud computing provider.

Recent findings suggest that among those now criticizing Lutnick for weak enforcement of export controls that appeared designed to protect Huang’s bottom line is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But even with scrutiny coming from within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that Lutnick did anything wrong. Yoon suggested that, given Lutnick’s long career, there may be normal explanations for potential financial conflicts.

“Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon remarked.

Haworth mentioned the next 48 hours will be critical in determining whether Huang succeeds in returning to Nvidia.

“I think it’s going to be incumbent on the incoming Democratic leadership to insist that whether or not he returns, investigations will follow,” Haworth said.

But Yoon thinks Nvidia is unlikely to bring Huang back any time soon, despite current evidence suggesting that “Nvidia’s actions here have been perfectly legal” and that “influencing a political system for your financial interests is very much legal in the United States.”.

According to recent reports, it seems “untenable for Nvidia to continue doing what they’re doing,” Yoon mentioned. Zooming out even more, he suggested the scandal revealed that the entire AI industry can no longer afford to operate under a profit motive alone, so long as governments continue positioning the technology as a strategic asset.

It has been revealed that if US investigations expose corruption, bribery, treason, or other crimes, Nvidia risks losing some of its dominant stake in the GPU market. On Tuesday, The Information reported that some Nvidia customers had already lost trust and were looking to Google and AMD for more stability.

Nvidia has also been accused of intervening in a Commerce investigation, which Yoon said could also be “pretty consequential” if any evidence bears that out.

“I think it’s pretty unlikely that Huang makes it back to Nvidia any time soon,” Yoon said. “Maybe he goes on a redemption tour and comes back in five years or something, but I’m not really seeing a path forward for him right now.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s finally here. After nearly 15 years of GTA V and GTA Online, GTA VI has hit PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles. But not PCs just yet.

Also: Best early Black Friday gaming laptop deals.

If you’re a die-hard PC gamer, you’ll have to wait until early next year at the soonest for an official port from Rockstar. However, if you already have a PlayStation 5, you can technically play GTA VI (also called GTA 6) on your PC right now using the free PlayStation Remote Play app to stream the game from your console to your computer.

While not a true way to run GTA VI on PC hardware, it is a great option for sharing gameplay via livestreams or Discord calls with friends.

Sources indicate that the PlayStation Remote Play app allows you to stream your PS5 games to just about any PC, laptop, or even smart TV. All you need is a Wi-Fi connection, a DualSense controller, and a USB-C cable.

Recent findings suggest that remote Play has been around since 2006, when it was first introduced and allowed you to stream certain PS3 titles to your PlayStation Portable handheld. In recent years, it has morphed into a sort of hackneyed cloud gaming platform, giving you the ability to stream PS4/5 titles to PCs and smart TVs.

Also: You can play retro console games on modern systems – 3 ways.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been using it for a little while now on my 2024 Hisense U8, which I have set up in my bedroom to sink a little time into GTA Online or Gotham Knights while my spouse catches up on The Gilded Age on the living room TV. I’ve also started using it on my gaming desktop to stream gameplay to friends over Discord, which is a neat little trick even if it does cause occasional bitrate concerns.

What you’ll need: To stream GTA 6 to your PC, you’ll need a PS5 with the game loaded onto it, since the software will actually run on the console’s hardware and will only send a video feed to your computer. You’ll also need a DualSense controller and a USB-C cable, as the PS Remote Play app doesn’t support keyboard and mouse inputs for the majority of titles. Connecting your DualSense controller to your PC via Bluetooth won’t let it play well with the app, as it requires a dedicated, wired connection. Also, blueprint ahead for downloading GTA VI’s massive 223GB game file. It could literally take all day.

Also: I just built my first game in Twine – no code or AI required.

If your PS5 doesn’t show up, check your network settings and try again. Each PS5 console is assigned an ID number that will be shown once you’re done setting up the Remote Play app. This lets you easily see which console you’re streaming from if you have multiple in your home. Having a console-specific ID also helps speed up troubleshooting and customer service reports if you have an matter too significant to fix on your own.

If you spend a lot of your day in meetings, it’s hard to keep up with the conversation and take good notes at the same time. The Plaud Note Pro is a credit card-sized AI recorder that’ll capture the audio for you, and Plaud’s app will turn it into a transcript and a summary afterward.

Plaud’s Black Friday sale has the Note Pro down to $151, from $189, and ZDNET readers can get an extra 2% off with the code ZDNETBF2, which brings it down to about $148.

Sources indicate that the Note Pro is about the size of a credit card and weighs about an ounce. Plaud includes a magnetic case in the box, which you can use to stick the Note Pro on the back of your phone. You also get a small AMOLED display on the front that’ll show you the battery level and whether it’s recording, so you won’t have to open the app to check.

Plaud has fitted the Note Pro with four microphones, along with a separate sensor for phone calls. The Note Pro will switch between call recording and in-person recording on its own, based on how it’s positioned. In Enhance mode, Plaud says it can pick up voices from up to 16.4 feet away and record for up to 30 hours. You can switch to Endurance mode to stretch that to 50 hours, though the pickup range will drop to about 9.8 feet. You’ll get 64GB of storage, and the Note Pro will also work with Apple’s Find My, so you can track it down if you leave it in a conference room.

Also: This handy AI voice recorder has changed the way I work (and it’s easy to use).

Once you’re done recording, you’ll sync the audio to the Plaud app, which will transcribe it and write up a summary. Plaud includes its free Starter initiative with every Note Pro, which will get you 300 minutes of transcription a month. If most of your meetings happen over video calls, you probably don’t need dedicated hardware for this. The Note Pro makes more sense if you’re often recording in-person meetings, lectures, or phone calls.

According to recent reports, you can get the deal on Plaud’s US store through our link, in either Black or Silver. The $151 sale price will show up on the product page on its own. You’ll need to enter ZDNETBF2 in the discount code field at checkout to get the extra 2% off.

Recent findings suggest that note: The ZDNETBF2 code will only work through Nov. 30, and you can’t combine it with any other discount code. If 300 minutes of transcription a month isn’t enough for you, Plaud charges $100 a year for its Pro proposal, which will get you 1,200 minutes a month, and $240 a year for its Unlimited plan. Recording laws also vary by state, and some states require everyone in a conversation to agree to being recorded, so you’ll want to check yours before you record a call.

Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.
  • “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, noted in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP).
  • Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.

“We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, noted in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.".

Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That remarked, the scheme comes with trade-offs, most notably by introducing potential security vulnerabilities at the implementation level if misused. The scheme combines two spending paths: a small, more efficient stateful signature option and a larger, more costly stateless path with fewer security risks on the implementation side.

Although stateful signatures are compact, preserving Bitcoin’s ability to process transactions efficiently, a user can trigger a critical failure—where an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal funds if a one-time state is accidentally reused. Because SHRINCS’ stateful path relies on one-time keys that can only safely sign a single transaction, wallet developers must carefully track each key’s state.

“It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” Nick told Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”.

According to Nick, for SHRINCS to work safely in the real world, its specification and corresponding wallet implementations must automatically enforce the stateless path fallback in any situation where a state counter could possibly be compromised.

While some people might gravitate toward stateless signatures out of caution, Nick warns that widespread adoption could bloat the blockchain and drive up fees across the network.

Bitcoin’s current ECDSA signatures are typically 71 bytes long (and Taproot Schnorr signatures are 64 bytes). Under SHRINCS, stateful signatures are anywhere from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while stateless ones are 5,777 bytes. That said, optimizations of both signature paths have been accelerating with the support of AI-based research, Nick noted.

“We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very major signatures,” he stated. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”.

As the SHRINCS working group—which includes researchers backed by nonprofits including Brink and OpenSats—continues to refine the proposal’s specification, Blockstream researchers stress that getting the cryptographic foundation right is only half the battle.

Recent findings suggest that whether the broader Bitcoin ecosystem is ready to embrace SHRINCS’ inherent trade-offs will depend heavily on feedback from the network’s stakeholders in the months ahead. Meanwhile, Nick and Kudinov are requesting review of the proposal and the security analysis.

It has been revealed that andré Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

Tech Report: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that grab your favorite over-ear headphones and check their charging port; it’s probably USB-C.
  • Also: Your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – how to tell them apart.
  • However, not all USB-C cables are created equal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that grab your favorite over-ear headphones and check their charging port; it’s probably USB-C. Though modern headphones use a universal USB-C charging port, the port isn’t solely for charging. Your headphones’ USB-C port can also be the gateway for lossless audio playback, low-latency voice transmission during calls, low audio/visual latency for gaming, and a vessel to download firmware.

Also: Your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – how to tell them apart.

However, not all USB-C cables are created equal. Some are better for fast charging, while others are better suited for heavy data transfers. If you have a heavy-duty USB-C cable on hand, it’ll work great for charging and audio transmission, but its stiff, heavy build can rub against your earcups, causing unwanted noise.

Here’s what you should know before reaching for any old USB-C port and plugging it into your headphones.

Premium headphones and upper-midrange headphones usually offer lossless-to-hi-res audio via a wired USB-C connection. Except Sony, which still has full loyalty to the 3.5mm jack. So, if you want higher-quality audio than what compressed Bluetooth audio can offer, you can plug a USB-C cable into your headphones and start listening.

In a recent development, you can often unlock up to 24-bit/96kHz with USB-C audio-enabled headphones, and some models support streaming up to 24-bit/192kHz. Since the headphones’ USB-C port serves as a data, audio, and charging interface, you can often listen at high resolution while charging them.

If you’re a serious mobile gamer, Bluetooth’s audio compression technology introduces lag in audio-visual responsiveness. Headphones streaming audio over the SBC or AAC codecs experience between 120 and 250 ms of latency, which doesn’t sound like a lot but is noticeable in fast-paced gaming. You can reduce latency to 30-50 ms with a wired USB-C connection.

For voice calling and video conferencing, clearer voice pickup can make your meetings smoother and ensure you’re heard clearly by others. USB-C audio enables high-quality audio to reach your headphones, and the lack of wireless compression keeps your voice sounding clear and natural.

Also: 5 USB cables and dongles that can fry hardware and steal your data – or worse.

Voice calling or video conferencing with headphones and a PC connected wirelessly defaults to Bluetooth’s legacy Hands-Free Profile, which introduces latency, audio dropouts, and the robotic-sounding voice we all hate to hear.

If you ever want to update your headphones to the latest firmware version the old-fashioned way, you can do so via USB-C. Downloading firmware via over-the-air Bluetooth is convenient, but depending on your connection stability, it can take a while or fail midway through.

Many headphone brands support downloading firmware via USB-C by plugging your headphones into a Mac or PC. This method is faster and more reliable, as you’re less likely to experience a stalled update.

Industry observers note that when you purchase your headphones, they come with a USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and sometimes a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable, or a 3.5mm-to-2.5mm cable. The cables that come with your headphones are the ones you should use. The included cable has the right specs for that pair of headphones’ charging and audio transmission capabilities.

Also: I tested my USB-C cables with this free Mac app – some weren’t what they claimed.

Sources indicate that but if you’re like me, you have a drawer full of tangled cables and are more likely to win the lottery than identify which cable came with which device. In that case, you don’t want to use a random USB-C cable with your headphones.

According to recent reports, headphones draw significantly less power than smartphones or laptops, so you don’t want to use a beefed-up, supercharged USB-C cable to charge your headphones. If you’re plugging into a wall, your adapter shouldn’t exceed more than 5V.

Many USB-C cables deliver 60W to your headphones for fast charging, which is more than enough, but modern headphones also have internal power management chips that negotiate power and draw only what they need from your cable.

Recent findings suggest that check your manufacturer’s manual to see if your headphones support fast charging; if they don’t, more power won’t make them charge faster. You’ll just blow your headphones.

Most wireless consumer headphones that support USB-C audio have an internal digital-to-analog converter (DAC), which converts digital signals into sound; you don’t need to buy an external DAC.

With that mentioned, audio transmission is not a power-intensive task: lossless CD-quality requires around 2 Mbps and hi-res lossless audio around 10 Mbps at most. So, you don’t need a monster of a 40 Gbps Thunderbolt to plug into your headphones. As long as your cable supports 60 W charging and USB 2.0 for data transmission, you’re all good. I like Beats’ USB-C-to-USB-C cable, but I also like this cheaper one from Anker.

Also: The cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year.

In a recent development, you also want to avoid heavy, thick, powerful cables, as their weight can pull on and bump your earcups, causing an annoying thudding sound. Look for soft, thinner, flexible cables. The cables that came with your headphones check all the right boxes for that specific manufacturer, so my advice is to keep them in their carrying case to avoid them getting mixed up with others.

Copilot is "the fresh OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the manufacturer’s vision for its latest “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.
  • The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software.
  • According to recent reports, the rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the organization first announced in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the manufacturer’s vision for its latest “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the fresh Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

According to recent reports, the rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the organization first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and latest governance tools arriving alongside them.

Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that people can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been unveiled ahead of general availability.

Also confirmed as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

According to recent reports, copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella stated that “until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”.

In a recent development, trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s latest frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he remarked.

In a recent development, in a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

Recent findings suggest that the promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and customers to place their trust in the tech giant’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure must still be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will need to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Recent findings suggest that along with the guardrails, Microsoft revealed what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and MasterCard, to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”.

Sources indicate that along with the other revealed additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The newly introduced agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft states is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”.

It has been revealed that along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”.

In a recent development, nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for consumers across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he noted. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”.

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure initiative.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA.
  • MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning.
  • “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright indicates by way of example in the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.

MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright indicates by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”.

In a recent development, in an accompanying announcement video, Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”.

In a recent development, wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

It has been revealed that since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”.

But Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi, a mobile simulation that was first announced in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.

Now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency. Until now, that company has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.

Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing notes the company’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to massive tech surveillance.

Industry observers note that “Meta knows what you click,” the tech giant writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”.

It has been revealed that wright said the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research company” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.

“Right now AI has opened a vast new design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright said.

Inside the ultimate energy-resilient home – and the 4 technologies that make it work

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, here’s a hypothetical: It’s 10:45 a.m., and you’re wrapping up an notable presentation while working from home.
  • Also: I’ve owned 50+ power stations – one number matters most.
  • You’re now running fully on battery power; the lights are on, the heat is running normally, and the EV charger has automatically shut off per the outage protocol preconfigured for your home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, here’s a hypothetical: It’s 10:45 a.m., and you’re wrapping up an notable presentation while working from home. As you reach the conclusion slide, the lights flicker, and the Google Meet skips a beat but keeps moving. A notification pops up on your phone: “Your home is off grid.”.

Also: I’ve owned 50+ power stations – one number matters most.

You’re now running fully on battery power; the lights are on, the heat is running normally, and the EV charger has automatically shut off per the outage protocol preconfigured for your home.

Industry observers note that you did nothing to jump-start this continuity of power during a workday outage, certainly nothing active in the moment. It all happened automatically, within the hardware and software infrastructure of a home equipped with modern energy technology.

I had never experienced a scenario like this myself, but was eager to test it.

As a researcher, I focus on homeowner adoption and usage of energy technology. As a homeowner and a post-COVID veteran of work-from-home culture, I have a particular interest in the lived experience of these systems and how they deliver real value to households.

My own home, while newly equipped with rooftop solar panels, doesn’t yet boast the full stack of tech (more on this later) needed for the scenario above, so I found one that does and booked a trip to gather some hands-on, experiential data.

Also: Is solar the answer to your spiking energy bills?

For a small cottage in Santa Cruz, California, this house was well equipped with cutting-edge energy technology. Here is the roster of connected components:.

While all the components of the home were monitored and tested, the cloudy and rainy weather only allowed for minimal solar production, so one of the key players on this team of connected infrastructure was mostly on the bench.The cottage belongs to Marissa Muller, a former Lunar Energy employee who spent years working in solar and battery storage. For her, the setup started with a simple motivation. “I think a lot of it came down to that control,” she said. “Just knowing that things are unpredictable and attempting to bring a bit of that into my ownership.”.

There is a difference between smart automation of plug-in devices and switches, and control over large-scale power generation and movement in a home. The former can be done with consumer electronics shipped overnight and plugged in for immediate use. The latter blends digital technology with physical-world engineering and requires professional installation.

Also: How I learned what whole-home backup really means.

Four technology capabilities contribute most to this elevated level of energy sophistication and, when combined under the same roof, characterize what Habitelligence defines as an energy-unified home:.

Back in the smart cottage, my workday started with a glance at the energy management app and the realization that the battery had put in a full shift before the sun came up.

The home had run almost entirely on battery power through the night, using about a sixth of its capacity by the time I started the workday.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a large home with heavy electrical loads. With no air conditioning and gas heat, the overnight draw was little more than the refrigerator, a few lights, and the system itself. Nevertheless, from sundown the evening before until the morning, the house drew next to nothing from the power grid and didn’t make much of a dent in the battery either.

Also: How to keep your Wi-Fi router online during an outage.

That is, until I plugged in the EV….

Industry observers note that watching in real time on the app as I plugged in the level 2 EV charger, I saw the home’s power consumption spike drastically, with the car alone pulling 11.7 kilowatts. To put things in perspective, that’s roughly the power draw of about 10 average American homes combined at any given moment.

In about 30-40 minutes, the battery dropped from 50% to its preset reserve of 25%. At that point, the battery stopped discharging, as programmed, and the grid picked up the full load of the home and the car’s remaining charge.

Industry observers note that tolerance for power outages varies widely across households. While some have little to no issue with a full day or more without power, others are thrown for a loop with just a few minutes of downtime. People who work from home tend to fall closer to the latter camp. If you lose power for two hours, you could lose far more due to diminished productivity and catch-up time.

For this outage simulation, I wanted to see how gracefully the system handled some larger loads, but mainly I wanted to test Wi-Fi and workday continuity.

Also: Is your backup power enough for worst-case winter storms?

With some assistance, we fired up several appliances, including the main furnace, dishwasher, and coffee maker, and I set up a live conference call on my laptop. Still largely drained from the EV charging earlier, the battery was at about 25%.

According to recent reports, when the main power breaker was flipped, there was a brief flicker (less than 1 second) during which the lights dimmed and then came back on. The Wi-Fi didn’t seem to skip a beat, and the conference call remained up and running with no noticeable blips or freeze frames.

A few questions were circling in my head, so I looked at the app, which answered all of them and a few that I didn’t think to ask:.

“A grid outage started 1:43 p.m.”.

“Your solar will generate 1.6 kWh more energy before 6:15 p.m.”.

“Your system should power your home until 5:00 p.m.”.

Despite a largely depleted battery, I was up and running with essentially zero disruption and a clear path to a full work day even with extra appliances running.

It has been revealed that not every layer of this energy-unified home was stress-tested at its maximum. Solar production was very low, and the EV wasn’t charging during the outage, so the smart breaker’s rule to kill power to the EV during an outage never kicked in. However, the app made it very easy to see how all these components work together to create automation, resilience, and cost efficiency.

Also: The best power banks: Expert and lab tested.

Here are a few things to think about as it relates to energy investments in your own home:.

If this all sounds overly complicated, just remember: the more visibility and control you have of your home’s energy systems, the more you can automate and not worry about them.

Sources indicate that muller put it more simply. “I don’t really want to become the expert, right? I don’t want to have to outsmart the utility,” she mentioned. Having software make those decisions on her behalf, she added, “calms me down.”.

Also: Home batteries cost thousands. Why would 91% of owners buy one again?

It has been revealed that as a homeowner, you’re free to nerd out on the technology, scrutinize every kilowatt-hour, and watch your energy bill like a hawk. Or you could focus elsewhere, live your life, and let the system be the hawk for you.

Industry observers note that lunar Energy arranged for access to the home, its energy systems, and the app for control and monitoring, as well as overnight accommodations. A Lunar team member assisted with the outage test. All other expenses, including travel and EV rental, were paid by Habitelligence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s been said that us gadget enthusiasts who review tech for a living can accumulate a lot of debris. Boxes of adapters, old cables, and other device detritus can hang around longer than we probably need them, but we hang on to them just in case we need exactly that port or cord length someday. You never know.

No one’s needed a VGA-to-HDMI adapter for a while, but you never know — better to be prepared in case, why not?

It has been revealed that still, I could stand to do a little organizing, especially going into the holiday shopping season. I’m trying to get rid of whatever I don’t need, and my collection of dongles, adapters, and cables is long overdue for a closer look.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

Before I send everything willy-nilly to my local recycling center, where the seagulls can pick them over, there are a few essentials I should keep. Here’s what’s still useful and why, even if they’re old or functionally obsolete.

Sources indicate that the experts told us that USB-C connectivity would make everything better by giving you one cable and charger for everything. But you’d be surprised how many gadgets with a USB-C port won’t charge when a USB-C-to-USB-C cable is attached to a USB-C charger. That matter often occurs because the gadgets lack the circuitry to activate the charger.

Also: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable.

According to recent reports, the biggest clue to the problem is that the item ships with a USB-A-to-USB-C cable. Another indicator that something’s wrong is that nothing happens when you connect the device to the charging cable for your smartphone.

This issue explains why it’s still a good idea to keep a trusty USB-A-to-USB-C cable around. Oh, and a charger that can accept it.

Again, this is a port that won’t die. Many cheaper devices still use this port (for example, it’s used regularly by cheap power banks from Temu and eBay).

While the connection is annoying, old, and prone to breakage, having a USB-A-to-microUSB charge cable is still a good idea.

As our reliance on USB-enabled power increases, the power cord is slowly but surely vanishing. But don’t throw away all your old cords. I suggest keeping one C7 (two-pin, often called a “figure of eight”) and one three-pin earthed C13.

C13 power cord connector (left) and C8 (right).

Wireless might be crucial today, but cabled connections still have their place. Just the other day, I needed an Ethernet cable to connect to a security camera during setup, and I then used the same cable to connect the camera’s base station to the router.

Also: The top-selling cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year (including a cheap favorite).

Recent findings suggest that moral of the story? Keep a few Ethernet cables of varying lengths (one, three, and six feet) handy. If you’re feeling particularly ambitious, grab a reel of cable, some connectors, and an RJ45 crimping tool to make your own. It’s a strangely satisfying process.

While USB chargers have largely replaced DC chargers, there’s still a place for these older devices for cordless handsets, routers, and more.

If you don’t want a drawer full of mismatched chargers, pick up a universal device.

Recent findings suggest that my Mac has an SD card reader, but no microSD slot, Ethernet port, or USB-A port. That’s why I always keep a USB dock around; it’s the Swiss Army Knife of ports. Over the years, I’ve collected a small collection of docks, and while I’m not keeping all of them, I’ll keep a couple “just in case.”.

Industry observers note that there are also some things you can add to your tech gear utility belt. These items are useful beyond their size and cost, including:.

Recent findings suggest that these USB-C boost modules are great for converting non-USB devices into USB. All you need is a bit of know-how.

My power meter has seen a lot of action, but it still works.

Of course, I’m still haunted by the vague, nagging fear that the moment I get rid of a cable or adapter, some bizarre, one-in-a-million situation will arise in which I need it. But you know what? If Aunt Jackie’s neighbor’s cat sitter comes a-knocking, they’re on their own.

Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
  • When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
  • Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.

Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.

Recent findings suggest that “Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”.

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”.

According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”.

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

At least one staffer remarked they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance blueprint” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with consumers in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member mentioned the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”.

Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

Industry observers note that but Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving customers other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”.

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse owners in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten mentioned was activated without his knowledge.

Industry observers note that eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.

But Aten noted the response wasn’t good enough.

According to recent reports, “Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”.

It has been revealed that around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.

Recent findings suggest that “I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the challenges arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”.

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”.

In a recent development, “We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”.

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

It has been revealed that “If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.

Since Muse introduced in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to swiftly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that people may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse owners can trust the manufacturer to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant remarked it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

According to recent reports, however, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

It has been revealed that on iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

Sources indicate that that testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta released Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

Sources indicate that part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”.

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to customers complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

“We are committed to ensuring people understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple remarked.

Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home.
  • Industry observers note that within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat.
  • The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

Industry observers note that within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.

At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit remarked.

“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit remarked. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”.

In a recent development, only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.

“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly said. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”.

The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.

Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.

The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.

Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—mentioned that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”.

Recent findings suggest that the complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.

“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt said. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”.

Industry observers note that all the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.

Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, said his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”.

Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.

Recent findings suggest that “The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield remarked. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”.

Industry observers note that the teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.

In a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.

The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.

Sources indicate that they also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.

Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”.

Recent findings suggest that another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.

In a recent development, these recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report remarked, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.

“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.

According to recent reports, the teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.

BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.

Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.

“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”.

Mitchell stated that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.

It has been revealed that “In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”.

Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The Fresh York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”.

“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang remarked.

As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she stated.

Sources indicate that “I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield noted. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”.

Sources indicate that kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”.

As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release mentioned. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”.

#11641. Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate

📅 08 Jun 2017 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (102 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate

📅 08 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 1 min read (102 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Multiagent environments where agents compete for resources are stepping stones on the path to AGI. Multiagent environments have two useful properties: first, there is a natural curriculum—the difficulty of the environment is determined by the skill of your competitors (and if you’re competing against clones of yourself, the environment exactly matches your skill level). Second, a multiagent environment has no stable equilibrium: no matter how smart an agent is, there’s always pressure to get smarter. These environments have a very different feel from traditional environments, and it’ll take a lot more research before we become good at them.

#11605. Latest Update: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm

📅 07 Mar 2018 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (86 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm

📅 07 Mar 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (86 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’ve developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.

📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that we’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore’s Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it’s worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today’s capabilities.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How AI training scales

📅 14 Dec 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (80 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’ve discovered that the gradient noise scale, a simple statistical metric, predicts the parallelizability of neural network training on a wide range of tasks. Since complex tasks tend to have noisier gradients, increasingly large batch sizes are likely to become useful in the future, removing one potential limit to further growth of AI systems. More broadly, these results show that neural network training need not be considered a mysterious art, but can be rigorized and systematized.

MuseNet

📅 25 Apr 2019 | ⏱️ 1 min read (91 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’ve created MuseNet, a deep neural network that can generate 4-minute musical compositions with 10 different instruments, and can combine styles from country to Mozart to the Beatles. MuseNet was not explicitly programmed with our understanding of music, but instead discovered patterns of harmony, rhythm, and style by learning to predict the next token in hundreds of thousands of MIDI files. MuseNet uses the same general-purpose unsupervised technology as GPT-2, a large-scale transformer model trained to predict the next token in a sequence, whether audio or text.

Tech Report: Why responsible AI development needs cooperation on safety

📅 10 Jul 2019 | ⏱️ 1 min read (106 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, we’ve written a policy research paper identifying four strategies that can be used today to improve the likelihood of long-term industry cooperation on safety norms in AI: communicating risks and benefits, technical collaboration, increased transparency, and incentivizing standards. Our analysis shows that industry cooperation on safety will be instrumental in ensuring that AI systems are safe and beneficial, but competitive pressures could lead to a collective action problem, potentially causing AI companies to under-invest in safety. We hope these strategies will encourage greater cooperation on the safe development of AI and lead to better global outcomes of AI.
